sources.title: Brusilov Offensive (1916) | Description & Importance | Britannica
sources.notes: Article by historian John Swift. Uses operational description, not its precise casualty ranges or the deterministic statement that the Habsburg prestige blow was irreversible. Its 10 August endpoint is a narrower scope than the broader campaign convention.

sources.title: Georges Clemenceau | French Prime Minister & WWI Leader | Britannica

sources.title: World War I - Eastern Front, 1916, Trench Warfare | Britannica
sources.notes: This broader campaign account continues to early September. The standalone article dates a narrower phase to 10 August. The atlas deliberately uses June–September rather than claiming an uncontested exact final day.

sources.title: Russian Revolution - The February Revolution | Britannica
sources.notes: The fetched page includes the wider revolution narrative. Julian 23 February = Gregorian 8 March; abdication 2/15 March; Michael’s decision 3/16 March. October operations span Julian 24–26 October = Gregorian 6–8 November. No modern-calendar month is silently substituted.

sources.title: World War I - Italy, Italian Front, 1915-16 | Britannica
sources.notes: Distinguishes Italy’s declaration on 23 May from hostilities/entry often dated 24 May, and from the separate declaration against Germany in 1916.

sources.title: Vladimir Lenin | Biography, Facts, & Ideology | Britannica
sources.notes: Read editorial biography, not automatically generated Q&A blocks. The map does not add an unverified Swiss residence merely because exile is known generally.

sources.title: Vladimir Lenin - Bolshevik Revolution, Marxism, Communism | Britannica

sources.title: Vladimir Lenin - Marxist, Bolsheviks, Revolution | Britannica

sources.title: Vladimir Lenin - Revolutionary, Marxism, Bolsheviks | Britannica

sources.title: Nicholas II - Last Tsar, Abdication, Execution | Britannica
sources.notes: Yekaterinburg lies east of the atlas’s 55° longitude limit; death remains correctly described in prose and is not relocated or clamped into an in-map itinerary. The article by historian John L. H. Keep provides the precise abdication city.

sources.title: Paris Peace Conference | History & Results | Britannica
sources.notes: Independent reference for conference organisation. The Paris opening is distinct from the June Versailles signing; no single treaty is said to end every postwar conflict.

sources.title: Philippe Pétain | WWI Hero, French General & Vichy Leader | Britannica
sources.notes: Older biography has sympathetic language about discipline and political motives; that framing is not adopted. USHMM controls antisemitic legislation, collaboration and responsibility. Actual trial was for treason, not a retrospectively invented Holocaust charge.

sources.title: Second Battle of the Marne | German Retreat, Allied Victory | Britannica
sources.notes: The article labels the German offensive 15–18 July; wider campaign histories extend into August. Atlas dates the opening day and explains subsequent counterattacks in prose, avoiding unsupported end-date precision.

sources.title: Battle of Verdun | Map, Casualties, Significance, Summary, & Facts | Britannica
sources.notes: No exact casualty total is taken from the article. Uses established date and operational facts while qualifying the retrospective Falkenhayn motive claim. Distinct event ID from the existing 843 Treaty of Verdun.

sources.title: First Battle of Ypres | Facts, History, & Outcome | Britannica
sources.notes: Date boundaries vary with scope; the atlas uses this conventional wider battle window while NAM provides British operational detail.

sources.title: Battle of Tannenberg | Facts, Outcome, & Significance | Britannica
sources.notes: The museum timeline uses a broader end date of 31 August. Atlas uses the conventional 26–30 August battle dates. Olsztynek/Hohenstein is a regional anchor, separate from Grunwald 1410; credit is not assigned solely to Hindenburg and Ludendorff.

sources.title: The German Empire (1871–1918)
sources.notes: Resolved URL is the Empire history page, not a separately titled revolution article. Used for its actual final section. An announced abdication on 9 November is distinguished from the emperor’s later formal signature.

sources.title: Kobarid Museum: Permanent Exhibition
sources.notes: Museum identifies Caporetto/Kobarid as the final Isonzo offensive and documents the human and rear-area dimensions. Its 24 May Italian-entry wording refers to the beginning of fighting; the declaration event is correctly dated 23 May.

sources.title: 1914: Mons to Christmas | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Distinguishes preliminary counterattack on 5 September from the commonly dated main Marne battle on 6–12 September. Its British Ypres chronology starts 20 October; the atlas uses the broader 19 October–22 November convention from Britannica.

sources.title: 1915: Early trench battles | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Reject the unqualified claim that poison gas was used for the first time in history. Earlier irritants existed. For Second Ypres’s conventional end date use 25 May; NAM’s narrative extends fighting to 27 May. No precise gas casualty estimate is repeated.

sources.title: 1916: Year of attrition | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Controls the museum-grounded Verdun narrative together with Britannica. Omits exact casualty totals and treats the “bleed France” formulation as an interpretation of intent rather than a complete uncontested operational order.

sources.title: 1918: Year of victory | National Army Museum
sources.notes: The narrative avoids calling Foch a marshal at the moment of his March appointment: his marshalship came later. Armistice signing early on 11 November is distinguished from the eleven o’clock ceasefire. The museum’s triumphalist concluding language is not reproduced.

sources.title: First World War | National Army Museum
sources.notes: General overview, not the authority for exact individual battle boundaries or casualty totals.

sources.title: Gallipoli campaign | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Atlas event is specifically the land campaign, starting 25 April, while the preceding naval operations are explained in context. Eceabat is a peninsula reference, not an Anzac or Helles beach coordinate.

sources.title: Battle of the Somme | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Preliminary bombardment began in June; it is not confused with the 1 July infantry opening. Avoid exact aggregate casualties and avoid portraying every Allied sector as having the same first-day experience.

sources.title: Battle of Passchendaele | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Uses the wider offensive boundary through 10 November, distinct from capture of the village on 6 November. Weather is one factor among terrain, defence and command decisions.

sources.title: 1914: To arms | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Used alongside OpenStax for the July crisis. The museum’s British perspective is not treated as the whole European or global history.

sources.title: Pétain’s Paris trial and the history of Vichy responsibility
sources.notes: Robert Philpot interview/report, 1 January 2024, including an AFP photograph caption placing the trial in Paris. Used narrowly for documented city and trial context, corroborated with USHMM and Britannica for conviction and commutation.

sources.title: The Paris Peace Conference and the Treaty of Versailles
sources.notes: Reject its loose opening statement that the conference convened at Versailles: the formal conference opened in Paris. Article 231 is described as liability for Germany and its allies, not a simple claim that Germany alone caused every aspect of the war. The 1921 sum is not projected into June 1919.

sources.title: U.S. Entry into World War I, 1917
sources.notes: Government interpretation is corroborated by the independent National WWI Museum. The European map event is the documented landing at Saint-Nazaire, not the declaration in Washington.

sources.title: 11.2 The Collapse of the Ottomans and the Coming of War - World History Volume 2, from 1400 | OpenStax
sources.notes: Coverage and broad context only. The event distinguishes assassination on 28 June, Austria-Hungary’s declaration on 28 July and Britain’s entry on 4 August; it does not claim every great power was at war by that day.

sources.title: 11.4 War on the Homefront - World History Volume 2, from 1400 | OpenStax
sources.notes: Coverage cross-check only. Curie’s specific activities and itinerary rely on Nobel/AIP evidence, not a generic claim about all women’s experience.

sources.title: 11.3 Total War - World History Volume 2, from 1400 | OpenStax
sources.notes: Used for topic coverage and general context, with museum references controlling detail. Rejected its roughly 900,000 Gallipoli casualties and caption describing Churchill as prime minister in 1915. No disputed precise Verdun totals or cross-war Somme comparison is imported. X-ray imaging is not confused with radium therapy.

sources.title: 11.5 The War Ends - World History Volume 2, from 1400 | OpenStax
sources.notes: Russian Julian/Gregorian dates checked against detailed biographies and revolution reference. Reject the text’s inaccurate January 5 dating of Bloody Sunday and its suggestion of two years of royal house arrest. Avoid implying the USSR already existed in March 1918, or that all European fighting ended on 11 November.

sources.title: France: Vichy, persecution and post-war trials
sources.notes: Independent institutional corrective to the older Britannica biography. The narrative states that Vichy enacted its own measures and participated in persecution; military reputation does not excuse collaboration. No unverified exact victim count is introduced.

sources.title: The Treaty of Versailles, 1919 | Château de Versailles
sources.notes: Controls signing venue and date. Do not reproduce its deterministic “seeds of World War II” framing or imply every wartime leader named was physically a treaty signatory. The palace is not used to establish 1921 reparations chronology.

sources.title: Interactive Timeline | National WWI Museum and Memorial
sources.notes: Timeline boundaries differ from specialised battle histories. Do not import its June 24 Somme date as the infantry attack, its conflation of signing and ceasefire time, or an undifferentiated claim that all European fighting ended on 11 November. Precise dates follow specialised pages.

sources.title: U.S. Enters the War | National WWI Museum and Memorial
sources.notes: Used for entry context only; it is not cited as proving the exact Saint-Nazaire landing berth or unit order.

sources.title: Who was Anne Frank? | Anne Frank House
sources.notes: Read complete biography. The cause of the raid remains unknown, so no alleged betrayer is named. The current account favors February 1945 for the sisters’ deaths, whereas USHMM allows February or March; the pack says early 1945 and no exact day. Anne was transferred away before Auschwitz’s liberation.

sources.title: Surrender of Germany (1945) | National Archives
sources.notes: Read explanatory material and the full primary surrender text. It covers surrender simultaneously to western and Soviet commands, not a separate western peace. Walter Bedell Smith signed for Eisenhower. Existing Reims and Karlshorst venue markers are preserved without changing their source IDs.

sources.title: Liberation / History / Auschwitz-Birkenau
sources.notes: Read the liberation section and navigation-linked historical context visible on the page. Paired with USHMM for approximately 7,000 remaining prisoners and January 27. The geographic marker remains Oświęcim town, explicitly distinct from camp sites.

sources.title: Anschluss | Definition, History, & Facts | Britannica
sources.notes: Read the Anschluss article. A controlled April 10 plebiscite is not treated as free consent; it is distinguished from the planned vote that was cancelled. Unavailable USHMM Anschluss URLs were not marked verified.

sources.title: Battle of Kursk | Eastern Front, German Offensive, Soviet Counterattack | Britannica
sources.notes: Read article. Uses July 5–August 23 for the broader campaign, not just Operation Citadel. Cross-checked with Tank Museum. Avoids contested Prokhorovka losses and the claim that all action occurred in Kursk city.

sources.title: Siege of Leningrad | Nazi Germany, World War II, Blockade | Britannica
sources.notes: Read the siege account. Distinguishes a narrow corridor opened in January 1943 from the full lifting on January 27, 1944. No exact civilian toll is forced from differing estimates.

sources.title: Munich Agreement | Definition, Summary, & Significance | Britannica
sources.notes: Read the full historical article, not only FAQs. The entry distinguishes the September 29 meeting from agreement early September 30, and the agreement from Chamberlain’s separate declaration. Does not claim Czechoslovakia freely negotiated the concessions.

sources.title: Benito Mussolini - Fascism, Italy, WW2 | Britannica
sources.notes: Read the rise-to-power biography. The event spans October 28–31 to distinguish mobilization, arrival in Rome on October 30 and the new government taking office on October 31. Does not portray the appointment as a military capture of Rome.

sources.title: Spanish Civil War | Definition, Causes, Summary, & Facts | Britannica
sources.notes: Read the dedicated conflict account. The start is July 17 in Spanish Morocco, spreading to the mainland July 18; end is Franco’s April 1, 1939 declaration. Madrid is labeled a reference point for a much wider conflict.

sources.title: Joseph Stalin | Biography, World War II, Death, & Facts | Britannica
sources.notes: Read biography and researcher-date note. Uses December 18, 1878 New Style / December 6 Old Style birth evidence rather than the later official 1879 date; the person card displays only the year. No Soviet-era heroic framing adopted.

sources.title: Wannsee Conference | Definition, Date, Attendees, & Significance | Britannica
sources.notes: Read historical article. Used for date and participating institutions. Some page summaries misleadingly imply the Holocaust or gassing began after Wannsee; those formulations are explicitly rejected in favor of USHMM’s chronology.

sources.title: General Eisenhower signing the Berlin Declaration, Berlin, Germany, June 1945 | The Digital Collections of the National WWII Museum : Oral Histories
sources.notes: Read museum catalog and original caption. Caption explicitly dates the event June 5; catalog/OWI release date June 15 is not mistaken for the event date. This is the assumption-of-authority declaration, not either May surrender ceremony.

sources.title: Chronologies | Eisenhower Presidential Library
sources.notes: Read chronology. It directly names London for May/June 1942 and Frankfurt for military governorship shortly after surrender. Biography uses coalition command, NATO and presidential service without inventing a route through battlefields he did not personally visit.

sources.title: Charles de Gaulle | Élysée
sources.notes: Read official chronology. Confirms June 18, 1940 appeal, August 25, 1944 Paris speech and June 16, 1946 Bayeux speech. Avoided the English page’s erroneous “President” wording for June 1, 1958 and its inaccurate Évian agreement date; the pack uses only a general 1958 return and later Algerian independence.

sources.title: Bayeux — geographic reference
sources.notes: Read coordinate header: 49.2794 N,0.7028 W; stored [-0.703,49.279]. Used only for geography. De Gaulle’s presence and speech date come from the Élysée chronology.

sources.title: Dunkirk — geographic reference
sources.notes: Read the coordinate header: 51.0383 N, 2.377500 E; stored [2.378,51.038]. This general-reference page is used only for geography, not as a historical citation.

sources.title: Natural Earth — 1:10m Populated Places
sources.notes: Downloaded and parsed public Natural Earth ne_10m_populated_places GeoJSON. Coordinates rounded to three decimals to avoid false precision. Country labels in the dataset were not blindly imported; Yalta is labeled geographically as Crimea. Historic claims rely on separate sources.

sources.title: Oświęcim — geographic reference
sources.notes: Read coordinate header: 50.03806 N,19.22139 E; stored [19.221,50.038]. Used only for the town’s geographic reference; historical and camp claims are sourced to museums.

sources.title: The Enabling Act (March 24, 1933) |             German History in Documents and Images
sources.notes: Read the translated primary legal text and introduction. It corroborates government legislation departing from the constitution. The event is dated to passage on March 23, while the body explains promulgation on March 24.

sources.title: D-Day | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Read D-Day article. Caen is an inland campaign reference, not a beach marker. The event distinguishes the June 6 assault from the following Normandy campaign and acknowledges British, American, Canadian and other Allied participation.

sources.title: Defeat in the West, 1940 | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Read campaign narrative and evacuation sections. NAM’s June 3 evacuation subtotal is distinguished from the final 338,000. Emphasizes navy, rearguards and Allied forces rather than attributing the operation solely to civilian boats.

sources.title: The battle for Italy | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Read full campaign article. Distinguished September 3 signature from September 8 announcement of the armistice, June 4 entry into Rome, and April 29 German surrender signature from May 2 effective surrender. The city marker represents the wider campaign.

sources.title: Victory in Europe | National Army Museum
sources.notes: Read the western campaign and surrender sections. Used to corroborate Paris August 25, Hitler’s death April 30 and VE Day May 8. NARA and the specialist Berlin article supply finer distinctions; the capital’s fall is not equated with all German forces surrendering.

sources.title: Remembering the Battle of Berlin: The Soviet War Memorial at Tiergarten | The National WWII Museum | New Orleans
sources.notes: Read the historical and memorial narrative. Uses its April 16 offensive start and May 2 city surrender. Rejects its broad Berlin/camp casualty aggregates and wording suggesting all European campaigns ended with the city’s capture. Civilian sexual violence is acknowledged without sensational detail.

sources.title: History Through the Viewfinder — The Siege of Leningrad
sources.notes: Read the museum essay on the Leningrad diorama and siege. Confirms September 8, 1941–January 27, 1944. Avoids adopting its broad casualty aggregate and its erroneous comparison of Stalingrad duration.

sources.title: The Liberation of Paris
sources.notes: Read the operational account. Used for Allied units, entry sequence and surrender at 3 p.m. on August 25. Caption dates of celebrations are not substituted for the liberation date; earlier strikes and resistance are not treated as a single unambiguous uprising start.

sources.title: Unsung Witnesses of the Battle of Stalingrad | The National WWII Museum | New Orleans
sources.notes: Read the survivor-based discussion. Supports the civilian dimension and Volga setting. The pack avoids repeating a single unverifiable Stalin quotation, treating one leader as the sole cause of evacuation failures, or adopting disputed bombing death totals.

sources.title: The Allied Responses to the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 | The National WWII Museum | New Orleans
sources.notes: Read analysis of Allied responses. Used with USHMM to distinguish logistical obstacles from political decisions; the narrative neither excuses German atrocities nor reduces Soviet non-assistance to an unqualified single cause.

sources.title: 12.2 The Formation of the Soviet Union - World History Volume 2, from 1400 | OpenStax
